thread.title: Tech Today: Tesla’s Brakes, Amazon’s AI, Hewlett’s Cash Flow

author: Tiernan Ray
title: Tech Today: Tesla’s Brakes, Amazon’s AI, Hewlett’s Cash Flow

organizations.name: hewlett’s cash flow scrutinized shares of hewlett packard enterprise

text:
By Tiernan Ray Updated May 23, 2018 12:23 p.m. ET Here are some things going on today in the world of tech:
Hewlett’s Cash Flow Scrutinized
Shares of Hewlett Packard Enterprise ( HPE ) are down $1.76, or 10%, at $15.65, after the company yesterday afternoon modestly beat fiscal Q2 revenue and profit expectations, and forecast profit this quarter, and for the full year, in line with consensus.
Illustration: Getty Images The focus of some today is not the revenue but the cash flow , which came in lighter than some would like.
Raymond James ’s Simon Leopold reiterates an Outperform rating on the shares, and raises his price target to $24 from $22, calling it a “solid beat,” but he also notes a couple of risks .
One risk is that year-over-year quarterly growth comparisons become “tougher” this quarter and next, he writes.
And the company risks missing its free-cash-flow target, he notes. "Combined with the negative FCF of $461 million last quarter, the 1H18 FCF run rate puts it well behind schedule for its goal of $1.0 billion in FCF for the full fiscal year,” he observes.
A number of “contributing factors” were cited by management, and "normal seasonal trends that tend to favor stronger cash flow in 2H,” he writes. "Although we see these expectations as reasonable, this still implies sharp FCF improvement in 2H18, and could provide an incremental risk."
In a chat by phone yesterday evening, CEO Antonio Neri , who took over from Meg Whitman late last year, told me the company’s “innovation is right on top of our opportunities,” including markets such as “hyperconverged” infrastructure, high-performance computing, and
Xilinx’s AI Ambition Means Higher Spend
Shares of programmable-chip maker Xilinx ( XLNX ) are down $3.16, or 4.4%, at $68.51, after CEO Victor Peng , who took the role earlier this year, held his first analyst day meeting in New York with the sell-side, during which his focus was aimed squarely at data center computing, and especially artificial intelligence .
The stock may be under pressure from the forecast that operating expenses will rise by 10% this year at $1.1 billion, higher than many thought. Morgan Stanley ’s Joseph Moore , reiterating an Outperform rating this morning, and a $78 price target, writes that he observed a “positive rate of change” at Xilinx at the meeting, and he liked the “company’s enthusiasm in pursuing newer growth markets."
He notes that the higher spending by Xilinx, unlike in the past, is "more directly tied to enthusiasm about future prospects” such as AI.
Defending Tesla Model 3
Shares of Tesla ( TSLA ) are down 41 cents, or 0.15%, at $274.60 as people keep discussing that ugly Consumer Reports review on Monday that declined to give the company’s Model 3 sedan the magazine’s recommendation. In particular, Consumer reports found the car’s braking system was lacking, requiring drivers to slam on the breaks sooner than with other luxury compact sedans.
Today, Gene Munster , formerly an analyst covering Apple ( AAPL ) for many years, and now a venture capitalist with Loup Ventures , writes on his blog that the criticism from Consumer Reports somewhat reminds him of what the magazine wrote about the very first iPhone, criticisms that "went on to be trivial."
" CR logged complaints about the inability to remove the battery, a headphone jack that required an adapter for non-Apple headphones, and said entering calendar appointments was not as easy as it was on a Blackberry.” Munster thinks that while the braking issue is “serious,” and needs to be addressed, other stuff is not that serious and this is a “speed bump” on the path of the Model 3 to “transforming the industry.” He remains optimistic about Tesla.
Recoiling at Amazon’s Face Recognition
Amazon.com ’s ( AMZN ) technology for facial recognition is coming under fire from civil rights groups, including the ACLU , according to a report from the A.P .’s Gene Johnson , who writes that the groups are upset about use of the technology, called “ Rekognition ,” by law enforcement officials to identify suspects.
For example, the sheriff's office of Washington County in Oregon, which uses Rekognition, has said "officers in the field can use real-time face recognition to identify suspects who are unwilling or unable to provide their own ID, or if someone's life is in danger."
The ACLU and other groups, writes Johnson, wrote to Amazon stating, "People should be free to walk down the street without being watched by the government.” Amazon’s AWS cloud computing operation released a statement to the AP stated that it "requires all of its customers to comply with the law and to be responsible in the use of its products,” writers Johnson.
Nvidia's Halo of Stock Influence
Chip titan Nvidia ( NVDA ) has a profound affect on other tech companies. Case in point, shares of South Korean DRAM maker SK Hynix ( 000660KS ) surged by 7% in Seoul trading, to 95,300 Korean Won, after the company inked a deal to supply Nvidia with memory chips, according to a write up by Reuters ’s Dahee Kim .
The stock hit a nearly 17-year intraday high price according to Kim.
